# Sharp centered-line mass versus radial-chord comparison

This is an ordinary one-dimensional lemma for the stationary-section route.
It does not give a mixed-integer depth transfer or the full scalar correction.

## Statement

Let f be an integrable log-concave function on the line, with positive value
c=f(0) at an interior point of its support, and assume integral x f(x)dx=0.
Put

    S=integral f,
    I=integral_0^infinity x f(x)dx
      =integral_-infinity^0 (-x)f(x)dx>0,
    L=2 sqrt(2I).

Then

    S/L <= sqrt(c).                                      (1)

If in addition f^(1/m) is concave on its positive interval, for an integer
m>=1, then

    sqrt[c(m+2)/(2(m+1))] <= S/L <= sqrt(c).               (2)

Both constants are sharp. A centered uniform interval gives equality in
(1); f(x)=c(1-|x|/a)_+^m gives equality in the left side of (2).

For m=0 interpreted as a constant density on a centered interval, both
bounds coincide at sqrt(c). For arbitrary log-concave f the lower constant
is sqrt(c/2), attained by a centered two-sided exponential.

Integrable log-concavity guarantees finite first moments here. On each
unbounded positive ray, integrability supplies a point b with f(b)<f(0)/2.
Concavity of log f on the segment from0 to x>=b then gives
f(x)<=f(0) exp[-(log 2)x/b]. A bounded positive ray requires no tail
estimate. Apply the same argument to the opposite ray. Local boundedness
follows from continuity of the finite concave logarithm in the support
interior, with one-sided concavity bounding any finite endpoint.

## 1. An elementary entropy-width inequality

Set

    F(t)=t log(t)-t+1,       t>0,
    G(t)=(t+1)/2 - integral_0^1 t^s ds.

The integral is (t-1)/log(t), continuously interpreted at t=1. Both F,G
and their first derivatives vanish at1. They have positive second
 derivatives, and

    G''(t)/F''(t)
      =integral_0^1 s(1-s)t^(s-1)ds

is decreasing in t. Consequently G(t)/F(t) is decreasing on (0,infinity).
Here is an explicit integral justification of the consequence. For t>1,
G/F is the average of the decreasing function r=G''/F'' with positive
weights (t-x)F''(x) on1<x<t. As t increases, the ratio of the new weight
to the old weight on their common interval is (t_new-x)/(t_old-x), an
increasing function of x; the newly added interval has still larger x.
A positive weight change with increasing density reduces the mean of a
decreasing function. This last assertion follows by expanding the
covariance into the double integral of
(r(x)-r(y))(k(x)-k(y)), which is nonpositive.
For0<t<1 use the weights (x-t)F''(x) on t<x<1. As t increases, the lowest
x interval is removed and the relative density (x-t_new)/(x-t_old)
increases in x; the same argument applies. The common limiting ratio at1
is r(1)=1/6. Thus monotonicity holds across1 as well.

For0<u<1, let a(u) in(0,1), b(u)>1 be the two solutions of F(t)=u,
and put w(u)=b(u)-a(u). Write A=-log a, B=log b. Differentiation gives

    w'=1/A+1/B,
    2u w'=2[w-(b-1)/B+(1-a)/A].

The monotonicity just proved gives G(b)<=G(a). On substituting the
formula for G, this is precisely

    (b-1)/B-(1-a)/A >= w/2.

Hence 2u w'<=w, so w/sqrt(u) is nonincreasing. The expansion
F(1+t)=t^2/2+O(t^3) shows its limit at u=0 is2sqrt(2). Therefore

    (b(u)-a(u))^2 <=8u.                                  (3)

The endpoint u=1 follows by continuity, with a=0 and b=e.

## 2. A tangent envelope and a bathtub bound prove the upper estimate

Divide f by c, so it suffices to prove S<=sqrt(8I) when f(0)=1.
A finite concave logarithm at an interior point has a finite supporting
slope s, and hence

    f(x)<=exp(sx) for all x in the positive support,

with the same inequality automatic outside it. Reflect x if necessary so
s>=0. If s=0, f<=1; on each halfline a density bounded by1 with first
moment I has mass at most sqrt(2I), by filling the nearest interval to0.
Adding proves the claim.

For s>0, the negative-halfline first moment is at most1/s^2, since the
entire envelope there has that moment. Put u=s^2 I in(0,1]. Let A>=0 and
B>=0 satisfy

    u=1-(A+1)e^(-A)=(B-1)e^B+1.

The endpoint A=infinity is allowed for u=1. Among functions bounded by
e^(-sx) on the positive x halfline and having first moment I, the largest
mass is obtained by filling the interval[0,A/s]. Likewise the envelope
e^(sx) gives the filled interval[0,B/s]. For a direct proof, subtract the
filled candidate g from any competing density h. The difference is
nonpositive before the cutoff and nonnegative after it. Thus
integral x(h-g)>=cutoff integral(h-g); the left side is zero, proving
integral h<=integral g. At the infinite negative-side cutoff the bound
is simply the envelope's total integral.

The two resulting mass bounds yield

    sS <= (1-e^(-A))+(e^B-1)=e^B-e^(-A).

The values a=e^(-A), b=e^B solve F(a)=F(b)=u, so (3) gives
sS<=sqrt(8u)=s sqrt(8I). Restoring c proves (1).

## 3. A one-crossing cone comparison proves the lower estimate

Again set f(0)=1. First consider one positive ray with f=h^m, m>=1,
h concave, h(0)=1, and first moment I. Its positive interval has a finite
endpoint b: an integrable positive concave power cannot stay positive on
an infinite ray, since any eventual negative slope reaches zero in finite
time and no eventual negative slope would make it nonintegrable.

Choose a>0 so the cone g(t)=(1-t/a)_+^m has the same first moment:

    I=a^2/[(m+1)(m+2)].

If b>a, concavity and the endpoint h(a)>0 imply
h(t)>=1-t/a on[0,a], and strict extra mass beyond a contradicts equality
of first moments. Thus b<=a. On[0,b], the difference
h(t)-(1-t/a) is concave and vanishes at0; its quotient by t is
nonincreasing. Extending f by zero after b, the difference f-g therefore
has at most one sign change, from positive to negative. It cannot be
strictly one-signed because its first moment is zero. If the crossing
is t0, then

    integral t(f-g) <= t0 integral(f-g).

The left side is zero, so integral f>=integral g when t0>0. If there is no
positive crossing, the one-signed difference and its zero first moment
force f=g almost everywhere, giving the same conclusion. Consequently

    integral_0^infinity f >= a/(m+1)
      =sqrt[(m+2)I/(m+1)].

Apply this separately to the two rays, whose first moments are equal by
the centroid assumption. Then

    S>=2sqrt[(m+2)I/(m+1)],

which is the lower inequality (2) after restoring c.

For the log-concave limit, use the exponential cone g(t)=exp(-t/a),
matching I=a^2. Concavity of log f gives the same positive-to-negative
one-crossing argument, including unbounded supports; integration of the
moment inequality can be truncated and passed to the limit. It yields
integral_ray f>=sqrt(I), so S/L>=1/sqrt(2) after normalization.

## 4. Relevance and limitation

For a two-dimensional projected density f(x,y), the radial body defined by
rho(u)^2=2 integral_0^infinity t f(tu)dt preserves all cap fractions through0.
If a full line section has centroid0, its two radial integrals agree, so
its radial-body chord is centered and has length L above. Formula (2)
therefore bounds the ratio of the original section mass to this chord
length, using the common central density f(0).

These comparisons do not preserve the full centroid or the balancing
weights of a family of stationary sections. In particular they do not by
themselves prove the desired scalar correction or the exact OC constant.
